claims.text: Conventionally cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 has a fine, uniform lamellar microstructure.
A minor Ti addition combined with post-casting aging will form uniformly distributed nanoscale Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates along lamellar interfaces.
Solution treatment at about 1100°C for 1 hour followed by aging at 600°C for 2 hours is an appropriate treatment for producing the proposed precipitate structure.
Controlled heat treatment will restrict precipitate growth and maintain precipitates in an optimal nanometer-size range.
Ti-rich nanoprecipitates will obstruct or pin dislocations in AlCoCrFeNi2.1.
Dislocation pinning by the proposed precipitates will increase yield strength.
Ti-rich nanoprecipitates will restrict grain-boundary sliding and thereby limit room-temperature creep.
Ti-rich nanoprecipitates at lamellar interfaces will stabilize those interfaces against corrosion.
Optimized aging will prevent precipitate coarsening and consequently avoid loss of ductility.
The Ti-modified and aged alloy will have higher yield strength than the starting alloy.
The Ti-modified and aged alloy will have improved room-temperature creep resistance.
The Ti-modified and aged alloy will have enhanced corrosion stability under thermal cycling.
The strength, creep, and corrosion improvements will be achieved without sacrificing ductility.
The unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy has limited room-temperature creep and corrosion resistance under cyclic thermal conditions.
Ti concentration and aging conditions must remain within a narrow window to avoid coarse, brittle intermetallics.
Large deviations from the processing window may degrade ductility.
The exact optimal Ti concentration and aging parameters are not yet known.

Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in yield strength, creep resistance, and corrosion stability while maintaining ductility relative to a no-Ti control would falsify the hypothesis.
